title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage: ruptured berry aneurysm in ADPKD
vignette: A 56-year-old male with a history of polycystic kidney disease presented to the emergency room because of sudden onset severe headache. He has never had this type of headache in the past. Examination shows some nuchal rigidity. Neurologic examination is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

clues.note: ADPKD is associated with saccular ('berry') aneurysms of the circle of Willis. This detail is placed deliberately to point toward aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

An abrupt, severe 'thunderclap' headache (classically 'the worst headache of my life') is subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise. Onset is instantaneous, unlike the crescendo of migraine or the build of meningitis.

clues.text: never had this type of headache in the past
clues.note: A first/worst-ever headache raises the concern for a serious secondary cause (SAH), rather than a recurrent primary headache like migraine or cluster.

Meningeal irritation (neck stiffness) develops as blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges over hours. With a normal focal neuro exam, this supports SAH rather than a parenchymal (intracerebral) bleed.

whatMatters: ADPKD + sudden 'worst headache of my life' (thunderclap) + nuchal rigidity + a normal focal neuro exam = subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis. Answer D. Work-up: non-contrast head CT first; if negative but suspicion is high, LP for xanthochromia.
strategy: Two triggers: (1) thunderclap 'first/worst' headache + meningismus = SAH; (2) ADPKD is a deliberate berry-aneurysm risk factor. A nonfocal neuro exam argues against a large intracerebral bleed. Then knock out meningitis (fever, subacute), migraine (recurrent, pulsatile), temporal arteritis (older, jaw claudication, high ESR), and cluster (periorbital, autonomic).

eliminations.label: Bacterial meningitis - infectious meningismus
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: meningeal infection causing fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the headache builds over hours (not instantaneous/thunderclap) and there's no fever here; ADPKD points to an aneurysm. ✅ Correct if: fever + progressive meningismus + photophobia.

eliminations.label: Migraine headaches - recurrent primary headache
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a recurrent, pulsatile, often unilateral headache, sometimes with aura. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is a FIRST/worst sudden headache, not a recurrent pattern the patient recognizes. ✅ Correct if: recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with aura/photophobia.

eliminations.label: Intracerebral hemorrhage - parenchymal bleed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: bleeding into brain parenchyma, usually producing FOCAL deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the neuro exam is nonfocal; a sudden headache with meningismus but no focal signs fits SAH. ✅ Correct if: sudden headache WITH focal deficits (e.g., hypertensive basal ganglia bleed).

eliminations.label: Temporal arteritis - large-vessel vasculitis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: giant cell arteritis in older adults - scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision loss, very high ESR. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not a thunderclap headache and lacks those features here. ✅ Correct if: age >50 with jaw claudication and markedly elevated ESR.

eliminations.label: Cluster headache - trigeminal-autonomic
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: recurrent brief attacks of severe unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation/rhinorrhea. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's a repetitive primary headache, not a single thunderclap with meningismus. ✅ Correct if: nightly orbital pain with autonomic signs.

reasoning: ADPKD -> increased risk of berry (saccular) aneurysm of the circle of Willis
Sudden 'worst-ever' headache + nuchal rigidity = subarachnoid hemorrhage
A nonfocal neuro exam argues against intracerebral (parenchymal) hemorrhage
mechanism: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with saccular ('berry') aneurysms of the circle of Willis. Rupture releases arterial blood into the subarachnoid space, producing an abrupt, severe 'thunderclap' headache (classically the worst of the patient's life) and meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity) as blood irritates the meninges over the next hours; focal deficits are typically absent unless there is mass effect or vasospasm. Diagnosis begins with a non-contrast head CT (most sensitive within the first 6-24 hours); if CT is negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture reveals xanthochromia (breakdown of red cells in the CSF). Major complications include rebleeding, delayed vasospasm (days 3-10), and hydrocephalus.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Neuro > SAH: ruptured berry aneurysm, ADPKD/Ehlers-Danlos/Marfan associations, thunderclap headache, CT then LP (xanthochromia), vasospasm.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Map 'sudden worst headache + meningismus + ADPKD' to aneurysmal SAH; use the nonfocal exam to exclude a parenchymal bleed.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on nuchal rigidity, thunderclap, xanthochromia, circle of Willis, or saccular/berry aneurysm? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Meningitis (needs fever/subacute), migraine/cluster (recurrent primary), temporal arteritis (older + jaw claudication), and ICH (focal deficits) each miss a required feature.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: ADPKD + thunderclap headache + stiff neck = SAH from a ruptured circle-of-Willis berry aneurysm; CT first, then LP for xanthochromia.
